examples.text:
Useful way to test an AI agent before delivering it to a client (6 tests):

1. Source test. List the approved sources, which one wins when two disagree, and what it must ignore.

2. Tool test. Run every action it needs: read, create, update, attach, send. "Connected" doesn't mean the action works.

3. Access test. Make sure sending a customer message, spending money, or deleting data requires a human approval step.

4. Mess test. Feed it missing info, conflicting info, duplicate records, a broken tool, and an unclear request.

5. Shadow test. Real inputs, zero live actions. Compare its decisions to a person's before it goes live.

6. Repeat test. Same input twice. Same answer twice.

Then write down who gets alerted when it breaks and how they undo the change.

Installation is not acceptance. An agent is ready when the client knows what it can do, where it stops, and what happens when real life gets messy.

where 99% of businesses go wrong is trying to automate a BROKEN process.

AI makes great systems better and bad systems worse.

here's the workflow to fix a process first before adding AI:

1) Audit

Where does the process start?
Where does the final deliverable live?
Who approves it?
What blockers exist?
What happens when something is missing?

2) Optimize

Clean the boring pieces.

-file naming
-folder structure
-process rules
-review checklist
-backup sources
-publishing gates
-step owners
-access rules

ONLY THEN do you move on to step 3 which is

3) Automate

This is where we add AI, usually by turning the process into a Skill.

this process applies to content, sales, support, reporting, onboarding, proposal creation, etc. etc. etc.

If the human workflow is unclear, the AI workflow will be incredibly fragile and usually won't work at all.

A strong personal brand is THE most valuable business asset you can build.

One of the most interesting ways I’ve seen for building your brand/getting media placements is a free GitHub repo called Newsjack (https://t.co/klSYbnCxan)

Built by @elvissun, it’s basically a set of agent skills designed to turn your agent into a PR specialist.

Here's how to use it:

1. Install it. Give this prompt to your agent (I use a dedicated Grok Bot for this): "help me install https://t.co/itPF7SncMq from the github repo and setup a daily newsjack monitoring for my company."

2. Run /pr-strategist. It works out your audience, positioning, and news pegs before you pitch anything.

3. Run /voice-extractor. Give it 5-20 past writing samples. It checks drafts against your voice and strips the AI tells.

4. Run /newsjack-monitor-setup. Enter your expertise, topics, competitors, and RSS feeds once. Then /newsjack-detector flags fresh stories you have the credibility to participate in.

5. Run /angle-generator. It turns one fact into 3-7 story angles shaped for journalists (it won’t invent facts which is an important feature).

6. Run /find-journalists for a small, fit-checked media list. Then /same-outlet-ranker picks the one right reporter at each outlet.

7. Run /meanest-editor. It roasts your pitch like a veteran PR director before you send it.

8. Run /reactive-comment on HARO and Qwoted requests. It only drafts a reply when your expertise is a real fit.

Obviously you still review and send every pitch yourself.

But this is a really cool, free way to begin getting some media placements and backlinks to your website which is great for building credibility in your niche.

examples.text:
before you tell a client their AI agent is ready, try to break it.

Use this checklist:

1. Does it have one clear job?
Write down what starts the job and what measurable result it should produce.

2. Does it know what information to trust?
List the approved sources, which one wins if two disagree, and what the agent must ignore.

3. Can it actually use its tools?
Test every action it needs: reading, creating, updating, attaching, and sending.

"Connected" doesn't mean the action works.

4. Does it have only the access it needs?
Sending a customer message, spending money, or deleting data should require human approval.

5. Does it know what to do when something goes wrong?
Test missing information, conflicting information, duplicate records, broken tools, and unclear requests.

6. Has it practiced on real work without taking live action?
Give it real inputs, but don't let it send customer messages or make changes you can't undo. Compare its decisions with a person's.

7. Have you tested the normal path, every known failure, and the same input twice?

8. Are you recording the job, result, proof, human review time, errors, and value?

9. If it breaks, who gets alerted and how do they undo the change?

An agent is ready when the client knows what it can do, where it stops, and what happens when real life gets messy.

Doing your first AI project for free makes sense.

But doing it with no plan for proof doesn't.

Before you start, agree on 6 things:

Exactly what you'll do for free
When the free work ends
How you'll measure success
Whether you can use the before-and-after evidence
Whether you can ask for a testimonial or case study if the result is real
Which work will still be paid

At handoff, create a simple proof folder with:

The starting point
The change you made
The verified result
Screenshots or evidence links
One quote approved by the client

If you leave with no proof, no referral path, and no paid next step, call it what it was:

Practice.

you don't need an audience to get your first AI services client.

you need one buyer and one painful workflow you can explain clearly.

pick a market you can reach locally (in person events) or through your existing network (via text message).

then ask:

-what work waits?
-what gets copied by hand?
-what question gets answered every day?
-what slows down a lead, quote, or customer?
-what does the owner still carry in their head?

offer a short diagnostic conversation (free mini assessment).

then map the workflow, show the bottleneck, and recommend the first practical fix.

if the problem is real, the next step becomes obvious:

-clean up the process.
-organize the knowledge.
-build the smallest useful workflow.
-measure what changed.

client acquisition gets easier when the offer starts with diagnosis instead of a demo.

examples.text:
A business brokerage CTO told me half the owners he talks to have zero tech stack.

His firm talks to 8 to 12 businesses a week. Many of them still use carbon copy paper, fax machines, notepads.

Most of those businesses are unsellable, and the reason has nothing to do with AI:

-no systems, so the buyer is buying the risk that the owner gets hit by a bus
-cash off the books, so SBA financing is dead on arrival
-one-off jobs instead of contracts, so there's no recurring revenue to put a multiple on
-15 products when 2 of them drive 95% of revenue
-a website last touched in 2002

If a business has no systems then a buyer is really only buying the customer relationships, many of which go out the door the second the owner steps away.

Fixing that is a service. Reactivate the customer database. Install a CRM. Turn the jobs you just finished into a monthly contract. Make sure someone picks up the phone.

Notice how these are all OUTCOMES. AI can facilitate these outcomes, but it's not what we're actually pitching.

The consultant who can make a business sellable has a buyer on both sides of the deal.

examples.text:
21 agent setups in 6 months.

From a non-technical designer with no audience.

$0 spent on ads. Almost all from referrals.

@fhlcreative's model: install one AI agent as a digital employee, then get paid monthly to manage it and coach the owner.

Setup fee + a per-agent monthly rate.

He shared the whole playbook on the Build With AI podcast.

What I learned:

1. The product is the coaching, not the agent. Owners treat AI like Google. You get paid to manage it so they never have to.

2. Raise your price every yes. $500 setups became $1,000. Now he’s targeting $2,000 setups plus $1,000/month per agent.

3. Give the agent a value ledger. It logs every task and sends a weekly ROI report. One client’s first week: 63 hours saved, $6,300 in value.

4. Put yourself in the group chat. Telegram group with Phil, the client, and the agent. The client learns by watching him talk to it.

5. The agents handle real multi-step work. One prompt: find the invoice email, extract the PDF into Excel, save to Dropbox, send the link. Done in 10 minutes.

6. Uptime is a selling point. The best prospects tried agents themselves and quit when they broke. Phil fixes it before the client notices.

7. Free work is the referral engine. Friends in his small Georgia town told friends in Atlanta and Dallas. Now he has clients nationwide.

8. The pitch is one text. “I’m testing a managed agent service. Want to be a guinea pig? I’ll charge you less.” First client: $250/month.

9. Make the agent write to Excel, not its own markdown. A shared source of truth is the difference between a demo and a system.

10. Phil builds his agents on Orgo (@orgo). $29/month gets your agent a computer with pre-built templates. Phil’s agent handles the Orgo admin itself.

You only need to be one step ahead. If you’ve built an agent for yourself, you know more than the owner who never has. Charge from day one.
